title: Warning And Alarm Clarity Improvement
excerpt: Warning and alarm clarity improvement is the design of warning and alarm behaviour so that users can distinguish priority, understand the condition, know the required action, and confirm state. Creative Navy applies this capability across regulated medical devices, industrial HMI, marine systems, embedded displays, expert software, and dispatch or monitoring tools.

bodyMarkdown:
## Summary

Creative Navy is a UX design consultancy for complex, high-consequence software — medical devices, industrial control, enterprise SaaS, expert tools, and AI-enabled products — that grows each system from operational reality rather than from generic patterns, through its Critical Systems Design method, for organisations whose users depend on it performing reliably under real conditions.

Warning and alarm clarity improvement is the design work of making alarms, warnings, alerts, and other interruptive states distinguishable, prioritised, actionable, and recoverable in a specific product. The capability covers how alarm states are structured, how users notice them, how users silence or acknowledge them, how resolved conditions are shown, and how nuisance alarms are reduced.

Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method treats alarm clarity as a product-specific operating problem, not as the visual styling of warning components after the screen architecture is already fixed. In the documented engagements, alarm clarity work includes priority tiering, root-cause hierarchy, redundant cues, warning architecture, typed alert queues, acknowledgement semantics, and action-oriented warning content.

## When warning and alarm clarity improvement is needed

Warning and alarm clarity improvement is needed when the product can technically signal a condition but users cannot reliably interpret priority, source, meaning, or required action. In the documented cases, the failure patterns include colour-only warning states, too many low-priority alarms, non-actionable error codes, missing recovery indication, unclear acknowledgement behaviour, and warning overlays added after the main screen architecture was designed.

Alert fatigue and alarm fatigue are central risks. The documented vocabulary defines alert fatigue as the desensitisation that occurs when users encounter too many alarms or too many low-priority alarms. False positives and nuisance alarms are described as primary drivers of alert fatigue, and the Gericke case uses repeat-alarm rate as a process-industry measure of nuisance-alarm burden.

Actionability is also a recurring boundary. An actionable warning communicates both the problem and what to do about it. In time-pressured environments, a warning that communicates a problem without a next action is not actionable. The Gexcon CFD simulation case applies this principle to expert software: errors completed silently and produced valid-looking outputs, so warnings had to interrupt the workflow and specify the error, its location in the configuration, and the corrective action.

Environmental conditions can make ordinary warning cues unreliable. In the deSoutter Medical / Zethon work, benchmarking found that most of the 6 comparable benchmarked devices used colour as the primary, and often sole, indicator of device state and warning conditions. The documented concern was operating theatre lighting variability, where surgical headlights and overhead illumination can make colour coding unreliable.

## What Creative Navy designs in warning and alarm clarity work

Creative Navy designs warning and alarm clarity at the level of product architecture, state logic, visual communication, and operator action. The capability is not limited to component styling. In the Stromer embedded display case, the previous warning implementation had been added as overlays after the screen architecture was already designed; Creative Navy's redesign addressed layout and overlay behaviour, information architecture, and explicit structural rules for how warnings and interruptive elements relate to the screen.

Priority structures define which alarm matters first. In the Kardion MCS Controller case, priority tiering ranked alarms by clinical urgency and required each priority level to be unambiguously distinguishable. In the Cox Marine cluster displays case, the alarm problem was different: in a multi-engine configuration, a fault condition in one engine had to direct attention to the priority engine, not only indicate that a fault existed somewhere.

Redundant communication channels reduce dependence on a single cue. In deSoutter Medical / Zethon, every critical state and warning was communicated through spatial position, icon form, and colour simultaneously. The purpose was that failure of any single channel under operating conditions would not remove the signal. In the Cox Marine work, military night vision mode required alarm states to remain distinguishable under night vision goggles, which eliminated some colour and contrast approaches.

Acknowledgement, silencing, clearing, and resolving are separate design objects. In the MDU ship motion monitor, Acknowledge replaced Clear because nothing done on the screen changed the state of the ship. The practitioner-supplied bridge convention was that a flashing red alarm becomes solid red after Acknowledge, and clears itself when the condition is no longer present. In Schone Airspace Group Mission Control, acknowledging a notice is explicitly an attention state, not a clearing event; acknowledged-and-active remains a visible combined state until a source clearance event occurs.

Creative Navy's warning and alarm clarity work also includes queue structure and lifecycle semantics. In the maritime traffic software portfolio, operational alerts concerned traffic and equipment faults concerned the infrastructure producing the traffic picture. A single chronological queue was rejected because it mixed these populations. The selected model presented navigation alerts by operational priority and lifecycle, while equipment health appeared in its own typed view with an impact explanation, both cross-linked from a common event history.

## What the capability produces

Warning and alarm clarity improvement produces product-specific rules for alarm state, visual differentiation, priority, user action, and recovery. The documented outputs include warning architecture, priority tiers, two-level alarm structures, typed alert queues, alert-presentation rules, root-cause hierarchies, contextual alarm explanations, updateable error libraries, speed-conditional alarm logic, and distinctions between acknowledge, assign, resolve, dismiss, silence, and clear.

In regulated medical device work, warning and alarm clarity can produce hazard-traceable alarm-system requirements. In the Kardion MCS Controller case, requirements were derived from use-related hazards identified through the IEC 62366-1 usability-engineering process, with the alarm-system requirements governed by IEC 60601-1-8. The design requirements covered priority tiering, visual differentiation beyond colour, mute behaviour, and confirmable absence of active alarms.

In industrial HMI work, warning and alarm clarity can produce alarm rationalisation and root-cause hierarchy. In the Gericke industrial HMI case, secondary alarms were collapsed beneath originating events and probable cause was indicated so operators could address the cause rather than chase effects. Contextual explanations replaced raw codes, including the case where the correct action was no action, such as a temporary deviation expected during a refill cycle.

In expert software, warning and alarm clarity can produce silent-failure warnings. In the Gexcon CFD simulation case, warnings were introduced during scenario setup, at contradictory inputs, and at post-run error detection. The design standard was actionability: users had to understand what was wrong and what to do.

In embedded and vehicle interfaces, warning and alarm clarity can produce threshold logic and escalation rules. In Streetec kntrl 2, thresholds were derived from suspension certification rather than chosen freely, with permitted pressure ranges per axle, speed-conditional alarm logic, user-settable threshold values, and three independent interlocks restricting pressure adjustment while driving. In normal operation, colour stayed neutral so that alert colour retained meaning.

## Evidence from regulated and standards-constrained alarm work

The Kardion MCS Controller case is the most formal regulated alarm-architecture evidence on this page. The alarm architecture was shaped by IEC 60601-1-8 and by hazards identified through the IEC 62366-1 usability-engineering process. The design passed FDA evaluation as submitted, with no design changes required. The case evidence states that the alarm architecture contributed to the review satisfying identified use-related hazards related to alarm misinterpretation and missed alarms. Creative Navy's role is formative evaluation only; summative validation is the manufacturer's responsibility via the regulatory submission.

The deSoutter Medical / Zethon case provides specific evidence for redundant alarm cue design. The design response used spatial position, icon form, and colour together, rather than relying on colour alone. The documented evidence basis is formative evaluation under IEC 62366-1 and surgeon-reported design review feedback that state verification had been reduced to brief glance recognition. This is design review session feedback, not post-deployment measurement.

The Stromer e-bike embedded display case provides field-tested evidence for warning architecture redesign in a consumer vehicle context. EN 15194:2017 constrained warning device symbology and behaviour, including regulatory colour conventions. Creative Navy designed and ran a test in which 10 participants rode the bike for 3 days each on real routes in Munich and surrounding countryside, logging issues by severity on a 4-level scale. Before redesign, warnings accounted for approximately 30% of issues rated as requiring user intervention. After redesign, with 10 users using the same bikes, routes, and logging protocol, warnings did not appear on the issues list. A repeat test two years later again found warnings absent.

The Stromer case also includes field-measured eye tracking in actual riding conditions with 5 participants on the same routes. Average glance duration at the display fell from 4.32 seconds to 1.89 seconds, moving from more than twice the 2-second threshold established by road safety research cited as Klauer et al., 2006 and NHTSA Driver Distraction Guidelines Phase 1 to within the safe zone. Glance frequency per kilometre fell by 18%.

## Evidence from industrial, expert-software, and process-control warning work

The Gericke industrial HMI case is the documented industrial alarm-management case where ISA-18.2 and IEC 62682 are the governing frameworks. The legacy interface exhibited two central failure modes: no priority hierarchy and alarm flooding. Research found operators attending to the most visible alarm rather than the most relevant one, and a single fault could generate a cascade of secondary alarms handled symptom by symptom.

Gericke's client-measured repeat-alarm rate more than halved at every documented site within a confirmed single-variable window: 42% to 18% at a Swiss pharma site, 58% to 28% at an Italian food site, and 73% to 35% at a Swiss chemicals site. Fault-diagnosis time fell over the same period from 24 to 8 minutes, 38 to 12 minutes, and 68 to 20 minutes. The evidence is client-measured by Gericke, not measured by Creative Navy.

The Gexcon CFD simulation case is the clearest evidence for silent-failure warning design in expert software. Before redesign, simulations had 5–8 configuration errors per simulation, each requiring 4–6 hours of corrective work. After the warning architecture redesign, configuration errors fell to 1–2 and corrective load fell to approximately 20 minutes. The case describes both reductions as measured and identifies the warning architecture as a primary mechanism.

The European industrial automation vendor engagement shows a real taxonomy that was present but poorly surfaced. The reviewed process control software coordinated machining cells. The findings included an alarms table where an error row and selected row were both solid red simultaneously, a duplicated row, and an alarm list where severity was conveyed by a leading icon alone. The alarm detail already carried workpiece, pallet, timestamp, severity, numeric fault code, source classification, and failed operation; Creative Navy's design response surfaced this taxonomy through operator instructions, acknowledgement versus completion semantics, batching of related interventions, and a pre-warning state for tool lifetime below a defined threshold.

## Evidence from marine, dispatch, and monitoring systems

The MDU ship motion monitor provides a worked example of acknowledgement as distinct from clearing. The alarm binds to the rolling 20-minute maximum and minimum rather than the live value, because the live value may leave the band seconds after entering it. The documented meaning is: "That means that sometime within the last 20 minutes you are outside the alarm level." Acknowledge means the captain has seen the alarm; it does not change the state of the ship.

The Raymarine next-generation fixed-mount VHF work defines priority by consequence rather than arrival order. Four event priority levels were assigned: emergency, high concern, operational, and background. A five-step arbitration sequence runs between event arrival and display, covering classification, duplicate coalescing, arbitration against active incident and focus, presentation with permitted actions and sound, and conditional task restoration. The restoration rule states that no unsent action is ever replayed, and a restored call draft requires a new deliberate send rather than resuming into a transmission.

The Oceaneering dispatch panel case shows signal saturation and role ambiguity in annunciation. One flashing state carried two opposite obligations: a cart had been placed and should be dispatched, or a cart had arrived and should be picked up. The documented resolution used one colour for sending and one for receiving, with each flashing when action was required and steady when it was not, while red was reserved exclusively for errors. The flashing-discipline rule was one thing flashing at a time.

Schone Airspace Group Mission Control applies the same separation of attention state and condition state in a fleet-monitoring context. Every alert names its owning aircraft or service in the first visible line and keeps that owner across the fleet card, inspector, live notice, and history. Acknowledged-and-active remains explicit, and only a source clearance event moves the condition to cleared.

The maritime traffic software portfolio separates two alert populations by what they are about: operational traffic alerts and equipment faults concerning the infrastructure that produces the traffic picture. Controlled prototype testing recorded alert-prioritisation improvement from a legacy median first answer time of 80.5 seconds to 53.0 seconds, a 34.2% lower time. Correct answers moved from 6 of 8 to 8 of 8, and all eight participants were faster. The study was conducted under controlled conditions with sanitised training scenarios on a design prototype rather than a production installation, six of the eight participants had prior programme exposure, and no significance test or confidence interval is stated.

## Boundaries and limits

Warning and alarm clarity improvement does not mean every engagement on this page was an alarm-scheme design or alarm-management engagement. AIT heat pump controller work is limited to alert-presentation decisions: alerts overlay widgets rather than pushing the layout down, and the alert banner is the single exception to a non-interactive status bar. The AIT engagement did not design an alarm scheme.

Streetec kntrl 2 was shaped by regulatory and certification constraints. The documented work covers thresholds derived from certification, speed-conditional alarm logic, interlocks, and two-level alert escalation. No safety result was measured.

The MDU ship motion monitor should not be treated as evidence for a safety outcome or safety-critical credential. The documented system is deliberately non-actuating, and its alarms are comfort, cargo, and crew-safety alarms rather than immediate-danger alarms. No user testing, fuel figure, cargo-loss figure, alarm-response figure, interface credential, panel credential, regulatory credential, or type-approval credential is claimed.

The Oceaneering dispatch panel work sits in territory described by ISA-18.2 and IEC 62682, but no alarm rationalisation process was run and no alarm-management credential is claimed. The two-hospital endorsement is convergence of expert judgement from operations managers, not a measured result or validation.

The Raymarine work does not establish a safety, rescue, distress-response, collision, type-approval, certification, conformity, field, or acoustic outcome. Radio protocol behaviour, distress procedure, alarm audibility, and final conformity remained Raymarine's responsibility.

Schone Airspace Group Mission Control does not establish a flight-safety, airworthiness, or certification credential. The product is in test, and nothing was measured in flight.

The maritime traffic software portfolio study must not be generalised into live vessel traffic, radio, radar, or AIS behaviour. The documented result is controlled prototype testing, not production operation. The study percentages must not be averaged into a combined headline, and the work must not be described as eliminating operator error.

## Related pages

Warning and alarm clarity improvement is closely related to alarm management because alarm management covers the discipline, lifecycle, standards regimes, and characteristic failure modes that this capability addresses inside a specific product. It also overlaps with design for abnormal and degraded scenarios, error reduction and recovery design, state and status visibility design, cognitive load reduction, command integrity design, and research in complex operational contexts.
